description:
We are Sergio, Álvaro, Víctor and Guillermo, four enthusiastic space and software engineers in Madrid interested in space, the moon and space missions. We are thrilled to start this challenge and find the best solutions to the problems we are presented.

If you share our interests, or are excited to overcome the challenge, come join us! The best ideas require bold people... Maybe even a little lunatik.
summary:
LunaTik Finder helps scientists, students and space enthusiasts decide where and when to land on the Moon. For any place and any moment between 2025 and 2035, it shows where the Sun and the Earth stand over the site's real terrain horizon, and turns that into what a mission needs to know: hours of sunlight and of direct contact with Earth, the longest night and blackout, the time to the next sunset and Earthset, and whether solar panels and a battery, or even a crewed habitat, can make it through. 

Planners can start from a site or from their mission's requirements, filter the south pole by terrain, light, power and communication, compare candidates side by side, and see in seconds what a launch delay does. A first-person Horizon view puts the user on the surface, and an Educational mode turns the same engine into story missions in a re-imagined moon. Built on NASA/JPL ephemerides validated against JPL Horizons, it makes the real constraints of lunar landings fast to explore and easy to understand.

Because to explore the stars humanity has to be bold, maybe even a little LunaTik?
details:
Have you ever missed your launch window? Are you tired of sifting through hundreds of landing sites to find the right one? So were we, and that is why we built LunaTik Finder, a tool for scientists, students and space enthusiasts that answers the two questions every lunar mission starts with: where should we land, and when?

What is LunaTik Finder?

LunaTik Finder is a tool, and it lets you pick any place on the Moon and any moment between 2025 and 2035 and see what a lander there would live through: where the Sun and the Earth stand over the real terrain horizon, how many hours of sunlight and of direct contact with Earth the mission will get, how long its nights and blackouts will last, and whether it can be powered through them. Everything is computed from NASA data, every number on screen says where it came from, and the same results are available to anyone through an open API.

As scientists, we always look towards the future: the next generation. That is why the Educational mode rebuilds the same Moon as a world of cubes from the real LOLA heights, with the Sun and the Earth in their true places, and offers twelve story missions for children based on real ones, from Apollo 11 to Chandrayaan-3 and the Artemis regions. Each mission ends with a question answered with the engine's own numbers.

A tour of the app

The app opens on a 3D Moon built from LOLA topography and lit by the Sun exactly as it is at the chosen moment, with the real stars behind it. You can switch from the relief to real imagery from the LROC WAC mosaic. To let mission planners dig deeper, you can zoom into the south pole, where a detailed polar map opens. The south pole is a very special place: the Sun never climbs far above the horizon, a ridge can stay lit for days while the crater next to it stays dark, and the Earth rises and sets as the Moon wobbles. That is why it deserves its own analysis. The polar map shows 3D relief with live shadows, and you can colour it by elevation, slope, long-term sunlight, Earth visibility and permanent shadow.

You can also choose a date and time and let time run, watching how the shadows, the power generation and the Earth contact evolve at a specific place. A timeline along the bottom shows at a glance when the site is in sunlight and when it can talk to Earth.

There are two main ways to navigate the app: by site or mission, and by filters. In Study mode you search for one of 21 catalogued sites with cited coordinates, from Apollo 11 to IM-2, Blue Ghost 1, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM and candidate south-polar sites, or you click anywhere on the map or type coordinates. The place panel then tells you everything about that spot: where the Sun and the Earth are and how much of each disc is visible, the time left until the next sunset and Earthset, the share of the mission in sunlight, the longest night, the hours of Earth contact and the longest blackout.

In Mission mode you start from what your mission needs. You set hard limits on the terrain (slope, elevation, crater density, distance from crater rims and from past landings, staying out of permanent shadow), on the landing (Sun height and Earth in view at touchdown), on light and power (sunlight during the mission, mean solar power, longest night, whether the battery survives) and on Earth contact (direct-to-Earth time, longest blackout). Only the places that pass every filter appear on the map, ranked by a score whose weights you can see and change.

The Horizon view then puts you on the ground. The Sun and the Earth are drawn at their true size, the Earth with its phase, over the site's real skyline traced from LOLA, together with their paths across the mission and the stars. It answers the challenge's central question in a single picture: from this exact spot, is the Sun up and is the Earth in view?

Power is analysed in three steps, with increasing complexity and reach: First, a solar array analysis computes the power generated using real panel data. Second, a battery cycling analysis checks how a load is carried through every night, including the eclipses caused by the Earth, to tell whether the spot stays within the battery's limits. Finally, the app models a crewed colony, whose habitat heating comes from a thermal model and whose loads can be prioritised, ending in a clear verdict: it survives, it survives but its power keeps declining, or it fails after a given number of days. The radiation dose from open sky, based on LRO CRaTER measurements, completes the picture. Up to four places can be compared side by side, and a table of sites against landing months shows which dates still work when the launch slips.

How it works: our key technical choices

Using the real horizon From NASA LRO LOLA elevation models we trace the skyline around each south-polar site in 720 directions. Each skyline is traced 2 m above the ground, where panels and antennas would sit, and follows the curvature of the Moon. This is key as near the pole the Sun moves along the horizon line, so a hill a few kilometres away decides whether a lander has light.

Use of ephemeris data Positions come from NASA/JPL SPICE kernels (DE440), are tabulated hourly in the Moon's own reference frame and are validated against the JPL Horizons System. The engine subtracts the observer's position on the Moon to give the exact line of sight to the Sun and the Earth.

Open API at the core. A FastAPI backend computes everything and serves it through a documented API (Sun, Earth, power, thermal, radiation, filters, scores and verdicts). The web app is one client of it, and a line-by-line port of the engine runs in the browser to animate the Sun in real time. This gives fast and accurate results in an instant, which is key in fast-paced and critical situations.

Case study: what a one-week delay does to a landing

To put the app to the test, we ran a 14-day surface mission at the intended landing site of IM-2 (84.78° S, 29.13° E), with the instruments 2 m above the ground, for a landing on 15 January 2027 and for delays of one and two weeks. All numbers below come straight from our API:

On time, the lander enjoys almost continuous sunlight and only short breaks in its link with Earth. One week later, the Sun sets after about six and a half days and does not come back before the mission ends, and the longest blackout grows from a day and a half to almost six days. Two weeks later, a solar-powered lander would never see the Sun. A planner sees this in seconds by moving the date, and the table of sites against months shows which other site or date would rescue the mission.

The same case shows why the real terrain matters. Computed on a smooth Moon at the same coordinates, the one-week delay would leave only 150 h of Earth contact with a 187 h blackout, when the real skyline gives 200 h and 137 h. In the two-week case the smooth Moon promises 22 h of sunlight that the real terrain never delivers. The error goes in both directions, which is why LunaTik Finder always says which horizon each result is based on.

Final Considerations

Can we trust it?

We measured it, we tested it and we pushed it to its limit. The app shows the results on its Data & methods page. Against JPL Horizons, 352 Sun and Earth directions at 11 sites differ by at most 0.000026°, where we required 0.01°. Against the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal, 43 events from six Apollo missions agree within 0.066° in Sun elevation, and the Earth differs from those 1970s tables by exactly the parallax they ignored. Against LROC, the ground height we read at IM-1 is 2592 m against the published 2579 m, and at Chandrayaan-3 529 m against 532 m. Where data is missing, the app says so instead of guessing.

Benefits and impact

For mission planners, LunaTik Finder replaces a tour through several expert tools with one place where a site can be found, checked and compared, with every assumption in view. A launch slip becomes just a slider. Each scenario lives in the page address, so a science team and an engineering team can share exactly the same numbers with a link. For educators and the public, it shows why the lunar south pole is so demanding, and the Educational mode turns that into missions a child can complete. Our goal is to make these trade-offs understandable to anyone and to give future CLPS and Artemis planners a fast, transparent first look.

What makes it creative

LunaTik Finder does not stop at a chart: it puts you on the surface and lets you watch the sky over the real skyline. It climbs from "where is the Sun?" all the way to "can a crewed colony survive the night here?", and the same engine powers both a professional planning tool and a cube-world game.

Built with

The project is written in Python and TypeScript. The backend uses FastAPI, NumPy and SpiceyPy (NASA NAIF SPICE), with rasterio and pyproj for the terrain data. The frontend uses React, Vite and Three.js. Our data comes from NASA: JPL SPICE and Horizons, LRO LOLA topography and polar illumination from NASA GSFC, the LROC WAC mosaic through NASA Moon Trek, LRO CRaTER and the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal, complemented by the Robbins crater database (USGS) and the Yale Bright Star Catalogue (NASA HEASARC). No special hardware was needed. Claude, from Anthropic, assisted with research, code and documentation under the team's direction.

Extra

Accuracy came first: every value has a cited source, and what no dataset provides is reported as unknown instead of guessed. We kept the known gaps visible, such as the missing boulder data and the coarse resolution of the screening grids. We designed for planners, students and children at the same time, and aimed for accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA, full keyboard control, a table behind every chart). And we made the code, the data and the API public, so anyone can check our results or build on them to keep contributing to humanity's future across the stars.

AI DECLARATION
We used AI assistants for research and information gathering, data analysis and interpretation, coding, debugging and troubleshooting, and re-writing, editing and translation of our docs and form texts. AI also helped with visual design and image creation. All decisions about the solution were made by the team, and every result was reviewed and checked against cited NASA data.
